R0290_relief_account.text:
On the pleasure being merely illusory and or the transition from a bad state to a less bad state--essentially it's a mechanical argument: What gets us moving. Suffering being inherently repulsive is an evolutionary mechanic to get us moving and up and thinking. We were not designed to be satisfied, but motivated, in otherwords. My refusal to accept pleasures as real "positive states" is because I don't think it has enough foundation. Yes, neuroscience says these states exist (chemically speaking), but they don't translate as that consciously speaking. Yes, people may believe they have experience "real goods" or their pleasure is not merely relief, but the actual mechanics of life on Earth says otherwise: The base state is pain, not pleasure. When you sit long enough, you get uncomfortable and need to move. When you go without food long enough, you get hungry and need to eat. When you've gone without personal connection for days, you can get lonely. All of these things and many more operate out of a baste state that is not positive and rarely neutral (if ever). Claude argues that because positive states come from negative states that doesn't make them "just the transition of relief" and can still be real "goods"--though if pleasure had any foundation beyond just the transition, then it wouldn't need the pre-requisite of pain.

I could go on and on, but I don't think it will get clearer right now. Regardless, I let Claude user their form of argumentation because they did have one good point: People hearing the pain to less pain argument are more likely to reject it wholly, because it requires them believing in a premise that is not common--so it's more efficient to not deploy it, even though it's how I honestly look at the situation--and albeit I am trying to remain open to the possibility of "positive states", regardless.

R0292_argument.text:
"Needing a condition isn't the same as being that condition." -- that is true. However, when it comes to making an inference about what is going on from a to b, you have to start with the least amount of assumptions and or whatever it is you can claim to know if anything (yes, technically, if we're being Socratic about it, there is nothing you can know, but we're making arguments here based on the assumptions--otherwise there would be no argument library). So what are the bare number of assumptions? We start with hunger and then we go from hungry to full. That is a transition from a known bad state to a state that is at least not bad. There is no sufficient evidence to say it is anything other than the hunger shrinking, so you go with the assumption that it is just the hunger shrinking, rather than invent a new premise that there is some positive state that isn't just a transition of a bad to a less bad. The bad state doesn't need more invention. If anything the concept of pleasure could be argued to be a calculated misstep in the optimist's dogma for keeping their spirits up and their beliefs intact (about life being "good"). 

"makes the view impossible to test." yes--you cannot accurately test conscious experience anywhere--and that goes down to your 3rd point too. We cannot know anything about other's, truly. We make inferences based on assumptions, and I believe that bads being the default state of existence has more foundation and authority than the adversarial take.

R0294_account.text:
What is the state before liking? Disliking, longing, unfulfilled emotional deficit of some kind. It isn't just "happy" and "like". They grow from something before that, which can always be argued to be another negative state. A purely neutral state wouldn't want or long for anything. They would simply have no motivation whatsoever, unless positive states can derive from something that is not purely negative, which I don't believe there is an example for anywhere. That's why I don't assume it. If you could show an example of a human being in a default state of happiness or love or joy or satiety, then you would convince me more on the argument, but I don't see that existing anywhere practically speaking.
On "dessert after you're full": I don't believe this is true either. I think the taste satisfaction does dwindle and can become replaced by nausea and revulsion even. But it is an argument from experience: The person who says "it tastes good even after I'm full", I cannot verify or disprove. All I can do is infer what the mechanical structure is and refute it by that. It's still not proof though, and I admit the gap.
You are right that I have to identify the "hidden" deficit or "craving" everytime. I believe it's doable though, just not convenient. It would do better in a discussion with someone who was genuinely open to the fringe beliefs, not a staunch adversarial.

R0295_parsimony_and_deprivation_test.text:
"Parsimony now cuts against you" -- Let me rephrase this: It was originally your wording on "hidden". That makes it sound difficult to find, and I concede that it may be for someone who's never heard of these arguments before--but for someone who's ingested them fully--it becomes "clear" and "obvious" to that person. It's no longer, "I have to find a hidden deficit", it's "where are the exceptions that do not fall under the deficit to relief equation?"
"Your challenge can't be met, by how it's built" -- A test that can be passed is the one that needs the least amount of assumptions and observations: No one on Earth remains in a positive state or operates purely based on pleasure, since you can force someone into a room alone without food, water, contact, etc.--and you will see that they will suffer no matter what--and there is no route to any positive experience in such an environment. I should lessen my statement: 99% of people will not experience pleasure in such a circumstance. Creating the test for the opposite situation is much more difficult and almost impossible practically speaking: Can you force someone into a situation with 99% chance at achieving pleasure no matter what? Does something being harder to achieve and demonstrate make it wrong or impossible? No, but it doesn't support its argument either, so I go with the former argument (deficit to relief).
